text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Bonn defends itself against threats from Iran, agrees to maintain "cool-headed" policy.
- Annual report on German forests shows 20 percent of trees are clearly damaged.
- Critics attack plan by northern state of Schleswig-Holstein to sell cannabis over the counter.
- German crafts and trades see their sector in deep crisis.
- Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) threaten to scupper government's tax bill for 1997.
- Wave of businesses going bankrupt continued in August, figures from Federal Statistics Office show.
HANDELSBLATT
- Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi says Italy wants to be in Europe's planned Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) from the start.
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl writes letter to Iranian president urging him to stop deterioration of relations between Bonn and Tehran.
- Mortgage interest rates continue to fall.
- Defence technology companies prepare for fundamental restructuring in their sector.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Pension contributions rise to 20.3 percent for 1997.
- More than half of German trees are damaged in some way, report shows.
- Shares in newly-privatised Deutsche Telekom continue to rise.
- Politicians in regional state of Hesse demand resignation of top judge over allegations he also carried out highly-paid work for major trade union.
- Trend towards less shops with larger space in German retail industry, survey shows.
DIE WELT
- Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel warns Iran against escalating row with Bonn.
- Cabinet agrees pension contribution rises.
- Germany and Netherlands want to introduce European Union general secretary responsible for common foreign and security policy.
- Economics Minister says plans for Expo 2000 in Hanover are on schedule.
